body.statement:
There exist constants \(k,K>0\), independent of \(n\) and of the schedule-independent assignment law \(\mathcal D\), such that the broad complete-schedule prior satisfies
\[
\inf_{\widehat\tau}
\mathbb E_{z\sim\Pi_{B,n}}R_n(\mathcal D,\widehat\tau;z)
\geq \frac{1+k\|\bar q(\mathcal D)-q^\star\|^2}{n}
-K n^{-9/8}.
\]
The inequality remains valid when one or more expected arm shares are zero.
body.proof_tex:
The density \(w(v)=15(1-v^2)^2/16\) satisfies
\[
\int_{-1}^1\frac{w'(v)^2}{w(v)}\,dv
=\int_{-1}^1 15v^2\,dv=10.
\]
Since \(P_a=1/2+\varepsilon_nV_a\), the prior information for \(P_a\) is
\[
\frac{10}{\varepsilon_n^2}=160n^{1/2}.
\]
Conditional on \(P=(P_1,P_2,P_3)\) and \(A\), the observed outcomes are independent Bernoulli variables.  Their expected information matrix is diagonal, with \(a\)-th entry
\[
\kappa_n\,\mathbb E_{\mathcal D}r_a,\qquad
\kappa_n=\mathbb E\{P_a(1-P_a)\}^{-1}=4+O(n^{-1/2}),
\]
uniformly because \(P_a\in[1/4,3/4]\).

Let \(\beta(P)=\sum_ac_aP_a\).  Applying integration by parts separately in the three compact prior coordinates and optimizing the resulting vector Cauchy--Schwarz inequality gives
\[
\inf_D\mathbb E(D-\beta)^2
\geq
\sum_{a=1}^3
\frac{c_a^2}{\kappa_n\,\mathbb E_{\mathcal D}r_a+160n^{1/2}}.
\tag{1}
\]
This is the multivariate information inequality: its numerator is the gradient \(c\), and the diagonal denominator is the sum of likelihood and prior information.

The right side of (1), multiplied by \(n\), converges on the interior simplex to
\[
F(q)=\frac14\sum_a\frac{c_a^2}{q_a}.
\]
Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\[
F(q)\geq\frac14\left(\sum_a|c_a|\right)^2=1,
\]
with equality only at \(q=q^\star\).  Its Hessian is positive definite on the tangent plane at \(q^\star\).  Compactness away from \(q^\star\), together with divergence at the boundary before the \(n^{-1/2}\) ridge is applied, therefore supplies constants \(k_0,K_0>0\) such that, uniformly on the closed simplex,
\[
\sum_a
\frac{c_a^2}{\kappa_n n q_a+160n^{1/2}}
\geq \frac{1+2k_0\|q-q^\star\|^2}{n}-K_0n^{-3/2}.
\tag{2}
\]
The right side may be truncated above by \(2/n\), preserving (2) after reducing \(k_0\).

It remains to transfer the parameter bound to the realized finite-population target.  Conditional on \(P\),
\[
\mathbb E\{\tau(z)\mid P\}=\beta(P).
\]
Because \(\sum_ac_a=0\), the unit contrast \(\mu(t_i)\) vanishes unless \(U_i\) lies between \(\min_aP_a\) and \(\max_aP_a\), an interval of length at most \(2\varepsilon_n\).  Hence
\[
\mathbb E\{\tau(z)-\beta(P)\}^2
\leq\frac{2\varepsilon_n}{n}=O(n^{-5/4}).
\tag{3}
\]
The \(L^2\) triangle inequality, (1)--(3), and the \(O(n^{-1/2})\) upper truncation of the square root give
\[
\inf_D\|D-\tau\|_2
\geq
\left\{\frac{1+2k_0\|q-q^\star\|^2}{n}
-K_0n^{-3/2}\right\}_+^{1/2}
-O(n^{-5/8}).
\]
Squaring and decreasing \(k_0\) proves the claim with an error \(O(n^{-9/8})\).  The ridge denominators in (1) are positive even at \(q_a=0\), so the argument includes the boundary of the allocation simplex.
